title: Lourdes and Fatima as pilgrims
hookLine: the sick and their caregivers at the heart of the pilgrimage

cards: Evening at Lourdes, in the south of France. A procession is forming, and candles are being lit all across the square. At the very front, before the bishops and the choirs, come the wheelchairs.
Old men in blankets. A girl with a breathing tube. A woman on a stretcher, looking up at the sky.
Pushing them are volunteers, some of them teenagers, some doctors on vacation, some who were pushed in a chair themselves years ago. The crowd waits. Nobody hurries them.
At a shrine well-known for hoped-for cures, what stands out is the order of the line.

teach.h: THE SICK GET THE PLACES OF HONOR.
teach.b: Lourdes in France and Fatima in Portugal are shrines tied to appearances of Mary that the Church has judged worthy of belief. Earlier on this path, you met them as stories. Today, meet them as pilgrims do.
At Lourdes, the sick get the places of honor: seated at the front for Mass and processions, with the Eucharist carried past them in blessing.
Volunteers come from parishes and dioceses to push chairs, carry stretchers, help at the baths and serve meals, some year after year. Why?
In Matthew's Gospel, describing the judgment of the nations, Jesus lists what the blessed did for him, including, in the Douay-Rheims, "sick, and you visited me."
At these shrines, Catholics act that verse out in public, with the whole crowd watching.

What about cures? Some pilgrims hope for healing, and the Church takes reports seriously. At Lourdes a medical office examines claims, and the Church is slow and careful before calling any cure a miracle.
Some pilgrims speak of a different healing: peace, courage, a family reconciled, a caregiver who finally rests.

At Fatima, some pilgrims walk long distances to the shrine, pray the rosary together in different languages, and fill the square with candles at night. The sick are prayed for by name. The two differ in their stories.
As pilgrimages, they share a center: the weakest go first, and the strong push.

how: Dioceses and parishes organize pilgrimages to Lourdes and Fatima that bring sick people together with volunteer caregivers, nurses and doctors; the sick are seated first at Masses and processions and are prayed for and blessed.

games.q: what does “lourdes and fatima as pilgrims” mean?
o: shrines where every visitor is promised a cure
Marian shrines where the sick get the places of honor

games.q: you're a teenage volunteer at Lourdes. the evening procession is forming and you're pushing a man in a wheelchair. where does the procession put you?
o: at the very back, out of the way.
at the front, ahead of the crowd.
at the side, so he can watch.
games.why: the sick go first. the crowd waits for the wheelchairs to pass, and nobody hurries them.

practice: Think of someone sick, frail or stuck at home: a neighbor after surgery, a grandparent who no longer drives, a friend in treatment.
Picture a place they'd like to reach and can't easily, a church, a doctor, a park, a grandchild's game, and picture yourself beside them, letting them set the pace.
If you pray, hold them in prayer and ask for the courage to offer; if you don't, just hold them in mind.
